title: Concept
description: Concept-phase review of product requirements, interfaces, loads, regulatory scope, manufacturing and cost targets, risks, serviceability, ID handshake, electronics integration and battery constraints.

items.text: Every mechanical requirement traces to a numbered line in the PRD or customer specification
items.hint: Keep a requirements matrix with PRD reference, ME requirement, verification method and owner. Requirements without a source tend to be argued about at DVT.

items.text: Each requirement is quantified with a value, unit and tolerance or limit
items.hint: "Rugged" or "compact" is not verifiable; rewrite as e.g. drop height in m, envelope in mm, mass in g. If the customer can't give a number, record the assumed value and get it approved.

items.text: Each requirement has a defined verification method (test, analysis, inspection or demonstration)
items.hint: Fill the verification column of the requirements matrix now; it becomes the skeleton of the design verification plan.

items.text: Intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse cases are written down
items.hint: List how users will actually handle it: dropped off a bench, sat on, used as a step, cleaned with solvent. Misuse cases drive loads and safety requirements.

items.text: Use environment is defined: indoor/outdoor, operating and storage temperature range, humidity, altitude
items.hint: State operating and storage ranges separately in °C and %RH. Storage and transport extremes (e.g. a closed vehicle in summer) often exceed operating conditions.

items.text: Product life and duty cycle are specified in years and in use cycles
items.hint: E.g. 5 years at 20 uses per day gives the cycle count for hinges, buttons, latches and connectors. Without it there is no basis for life testing.

items.text: Target user population is defined, including size range, strength and dexterity limits
items.hint: Grip size, actuation forces and reach depend on who uses it (children, elderly, gloved hands). Reference anthropometric data rather than the design team's own hands.

items.text: Packaging, shipping and installation conditions are captured as requirements
items.hint: Transit drop, stacking load and vibration often govern the design more than use. Note whether the product ships assembled, in retail packaging or bulk.

items.text: Product mass target is set, with an allocation by subsystem
items.hint: Track mass in a budget spreadsheet updated from CAD mass properties with correct material densities. Mass growth is easier to stop early than to remove later.

items.text: Requirements baseline is under revision control and changes go through a documented approval
items.hint: A dated, versioned requirements document with a change log stops scope creep from silently invalidating completed design work.

items.text: Space claim (maximum envelope) is defined in CAD and agreed with the customer and other disciplines
items.hint: Publish a space-claim model with locked outer boundaries. Check the current design against it with an interference or clearance check.

items.text: Every mating product or accessory interface is identified with its controlling drawing or model
items.hint: Docks, chargers, mounts, cartridges and third-party parts each need a reference model at a known revision. Designing to a photo or a competitor sample is how mismatches happen.

items.text: Interface tolerances of mating third-party parts are known, not assumed from nominal CAD
items.hint: Get the supplier drawing with tolerances; vendor STEP files are usually nominal. Feed worst-case values into the stack-ups (see Tolerancing & GD&T).

items.text: Mounting method and mounting points to the customer's system are defined
items.hint: Specify hole pattern, fastener type, mounting surface and load direction. Confirm the customer's mounting surface flatness and material.

items.text: Connector and I/O access locations are agreed with EE and match cable and plug clearances
items.hint: Check plug overmold dimensions and cable bend radius at each port, including right-angle and oversized aftermarket plugs, not just the receptacle.

items.text: User interface locations (buttons, displays, indicators) are fixed relative to the envelope
items.hint: Lock UI positions early; moving a button after PCB layout costs a board spin and a tooling change.

items.text: Access requirements for installation, cable connection and maintenance are defined
items.hint: Check hand and tool access with a human model or simple clearance volumes in CAD, including fastener driver length.

items.text: Orientation, mounting position and gravity direction in use are defined
items.hint: Drainage, venting, cable entry and load paths all depend on which way up the product sits or hangs.

items.text: Drop requirement is defined: height, surface, orientations and number of drops
items.hint: E.g. height in m onto concrete or steel, faces/edges/corners, in or out of packaging. Get the spec from the customer or the applicable product standard.

items.text: Vibration requirement is defined as a profile (frequency range, level, duration, axes)
items.hint: Use a transport or application profile from the customer or a recognized standard rather than an invented sine sweep. Note whether the product is powered during vibration.

items.text: Mechanical shock requirement is defined (pulse shape, peak acceleration, duration)
items.hint: Shock levels often come from the end application (vehicle, machinery, shipping). Record the source of the numbers.

items.text: Static and user loads are quantified with direction and point of application
items.hint: Include lean, sit, step and pull-on-cable loads as relevant. State whether a safety factor is applied and what it is.

items.text: Impact requirement for exposed surfaces is defined where the product could be struck
items.hint: Specify energy in J and the impactor (ball, hammer). Displays, windows and thin cosmetic walls are the usual weak points.

items.text: Chemical exposure list is defined: cleaners, disinfectants, oils, fuels, sunscreen, sweat
items.hint: Name actual products and concentrations; they drive material selection and chemical resistance testing. Plastics like PC and ABS can stress-crack under common cleaners.

items.text: UV and weathering exposure is specified, including expected outdoor hours or years
items.hint: Defines UV stabilization, colorfastness and material choice. Indoor-only grades fade and embrittle outdoors.

items.text: Corrosion environment is defined (salt spray, coastal, industrial, condensation)
items.hint: Drives plating, coating, fastener material and galvanic-pair choices.

items.text: Water and dust exposure is captured as a target IP rating or ingress scenario
items.hint: Record the IP code per IEC 60529 or a plain-language scenario (rain, hose, immersion depth in m). Sealing design itself is covered in Enclosures, Sealing & IP.

items.text: Grip, carry and one-handed use requirements are defined
items.hint: Specify mass limit, grip diameter range and whether use with gloves is required. Validate with foam or printed ergonomic models early.

items.text: Target markets and sales regions are listed
items.hint: Region drives which certifications, marks and material restrictions apply. Adding a region late can force redesign.

items.text: Applicable product safety standards are identified and owned
items.hint: E.g. IEC 62368-1 for ICT/AV equipment, IEC 61010-1 for lab and measurement equipment. Confirm with the test lab or compliance consultant, not by guess.

items.text: Mechanical requirements of the safety standard are extracted into the requirements matrix
items.hint: Enclosure strength, impact, stability, flammability rating (UL 94) and accessible-part requirements need to be design inputs, not test-day surprises.

items.text: Material compliance requirements (RoHS, REACH, Prop 65 and similar) are flagged for all parts
items.hint: Capture them as requirements so suppliers are asked for declarations at sourcing, not after tooling.

items.text: Medical device classification and regulatory pathway are identified
items.hint: Class and pathway determine design control rigor, documentation and testing. Get regulatory affairs sign-off.

items.text: Applicable medical standards are listed (e.g. IEC 60601-1, ISO 14971, ISO 10993)
items.hint: List the specific parts and collateral standards applicable; each brings mechanical requirements such as stability, cleaning and biocompatibility.

items.text: Design control process (design inputs, reviews, traceability) is set up per the quality system
items.hint: Under ISO 13485, design inputs must be documented and reviewed. Retrofitting traceability at the end is painful and audit-visible.

items.text: Skin-contact materials and contact duration are identified for biocompatibility evaluation
items.hint: List every part touching skin, contact type and duration. This drives ISO 10993 testing scope and material choice.

items.text: Labeling and marking requirements (rating label, symbols, regulatory marks) are captured
items.hint: Reserve label area in the design and note whether marking is molded, printed or a label, and its durability requirement.

items.text: Annual volume and lifetime volume forecasts are documented
items.hint: Volume determines process choice, tooling investment and cavitation. Get the forecast in writing with ramp assumptions.

items.text: Target product cost (BOM plus assembly) is set and allocated by subsystem
items.hint: Track estimated cost against the target in a cost model updated at each review.

items.text: Tooling and NRE budget is defined
items.hint: Tooling budget limits cavitation, steel choice and number of slides. Know it before the part design commits to them.

items.text: Manufacturing process for each major part is selected with a written rationale
items.hint: Record why injection molding vs. machining vs. sheet metal vs. additive, given volume, cost, tolerance and lead time. Revisit if volume changes.

items.text: Process selection is consistent with forecast volume and cost targets
items.hint: Rule of thumb: machined or printed parts that suit pilot volumes rarely meet volume cost targets; plan the transition and its tooling lead time.

items.text: Tooling lead times and their place in the schedule are confirmed with suppliers
items.hint: Get quoted lead times for tools, T1 samples and modifications. Tooling is often the critical path to PVT.

items.text: Supplier strategy is defined: single vs. dual source, region, and assembly location
items.hint: Decide early whether parts are sourced near the final assembly site; it affects logistics, cost and supplier DFM input.

items.text: Key suppliers are engaged for DFM input before design freeze
items.hint: Early molder, fabricator or machinist feedback avoids expensive tooling changes.

items.text: Assembly location and assembly method (manual, semi-automated, automated) are assumed and documented
items.hint: Automated assembly imposes stricter part presentation and tolerance needs. See Assembly, Fastening & DFA.

items.text: Production test and inspection strategy is outlined, including end-of-line tests
items.hint: Decide what is inspected at the supplier vs. at assembly and what fixtures are needed; fixtures have their own lead time.

items.text: A technical risk register exists with owner, likelihood, impact and mitigation for each risk
items.hint: Review it at every design review. Risks without owners don't get mitigated.

items.text: Design FMEA is started at the concept stage for the key functions
items.hint: Begin with system-level functions and failure modes; refine as detail design develops. It feeds the verification plan.

items.text: Hazard analysis or risk management file is started per ISO 14971
items.hint: Mechanical hazards (pinch points, sharp edges, instability, ejected parts) need documented risk controls traceable to verification.

items.text: Make vs. buy decision is recorded for each major subassembly
items.hint: Off-the-shelf mechanisms, hinges, fans and seals often reduce risk; note lead time and obsolescence of bought parts.

items.text: IP and freedom-to-operate check is done for the core mechanism or architecture
items.hint: Search patents for the key mechanism before investing heavily in detail design; involve counsel if anything close is found.

items.text: Prior art and competitor products are reviewed and their known failure modes noted
items.hint: Teardowns and reviews of competitor field complaints show which problems the design must avoid.

items.text: Key technical unknowns are listed with a planned prototype or analysis to answer each
items.hint: E.g. mechanism feel, seal compression, thermal margin, drop survival. Prototype the riskiest unknowns first, before the full design.

items.text: Critical-to-function features are identified at concept stage
items.hint: Naming the CTF dimensions and functions early lets tolerance analysis, drawings and inspection focus on what matters.

items.text: Safety-critical failure modes and load paths are identified
items.hint: Mark parts whose failure could injure someone; they need higher safety factors, analysis and validation.

items.text: Concepts are compared against requirements with a documented selection matrix
items.hint: Score each concept against weighted requirements and keep the matrix; it explains later why alternatives were rejected.

items.text: Service and repair strategy is defined: field-repairable, depot repair or replace-only
items.hint: This decides whether snaps vs. screws, glue vs. gaskets and modular subassemblies are acceptable.

items.text: Field-replaceable parts and consumables are identified with their access path
items.hint: Batteries, filters, seals and wear parts should be reachable without destroying cosmetic parts or seals.

items.text: Disassembly for service does not require destroying single-use features unless planned
items.hint: Single-use snaps and adhesives are fine for replace-only products but not for repairable ones; record the decision.

items.text: Right-to-repair or regional repairability requirements are reviewed for the target markets
items.hint: Some regions are introducing repairability and spare-part rules, particularly for batteries; check with compliance.

items.text: End-of-life and recyclability requirements are defined, including material marking
items.hint: Plastics marking per ISO 11469 and separable materials simplify recycling and meet take-back expectations.

items.text: Sustainability targets (recycled content, mass, packaging) are captured if the customer has them
items.hint: Recycled-content resins have different properties and color limits; capture them as inputs before material selection.

items.text: Industrial design surfaces are received as a controlled, versioned CAD release
items.hint: Engineering should design to a frozen ID surface revision; track which revision each part is built on.

items.text: Class A surfaces are identified and agreed with ID
items.hint: Mark which faces are cosmetic and their grade, so gates, ejector pins, sink-prone ribs and parting lines stay off them.

items.text: CMF specification (color, material, finish, texture) is defined for each visible part
items.hint: Reference physical color standards or color chips and texture supplier codes, not screen colors.

items.text: Parting line and split line locations are agreed with ID before detailed design
items.hint: Parting lines visible on Class A surfaces are a frequent ID/ME conflict; resolve on the concept model.

items.text: Draft required on textured cosmetic surfaces is accounted for in the ID surfaces
items.hint: Rule of thumb: heavier textures need more draft per the texture supplier. Adding draft late changes the ID form.

items.text: Gaps, flushness and step targets between visible parts are agreed with ID
items.hint: State nominal gap and flush targets in mm; check they are achievable with the tolerance stack.

items.text: Appearance acceptance criteria (viewing distance, lighting, defect limits) are agreed
items.hint: Define cosmetic inspection conditions now so supplier sample approval isn't subjective.

items.text: PCB outline, mounting holes and component height keep-outs are agreed with EE and frozen
items.hint: Exchange a STEP/IDF board outline with height zones; check against the enclosure with interference detection.

items.text: Antenna keep-out volumes are defined and free of metal, metallized coatings and fasteners
items.hint: Get the keep-out from the RF engineer or module datasheet; metal parts, screws and conductive paint nearby detune the antenna.

items.text: Thermal budget (power dissipation per component and allowable temperatures) is shared with ME
items.hint: Get worst-case dissipation in W and limits in °C, including surface touch-temperature limits. Feeds Thermal & Structural Analysis.

items.text: Cable and harness routing paths are reserved in CAD with bend radius and connector mating clearance
items.hint: Model cables and flex circuits as solids at their minimum bend radius; pinched or over-bent cables are a common field failure.

items.text: Display, touch and button stack-ups are defined with the EE and supplier
items.hint: Include adhesive, gaskets, cover glass and switch travel so actuation force and travel requirements can be met.

items.text: Grounding and EMC shielding approach is agreed (conductive coatings, gaskets, chassis bonding)
items.hint: Shielding needs contact areas, coating masks and gasket compression in the mechanical design.

items.text: Electrostatic discharge paths from user-touchable surfaces are considered with EE
items.hint: Seams near PCBs and metal trim can let ESD reach electronics; agree creepage and ground paths early.

items.text: Cell or pack is selected with datasheet dimensions, tolerance and mass
items.hint: Use supplier drawings with tolerances, not nominal models; pouch cells vary in thickness.

items.text: Swelling allowance around pouch or prismatic cells is provided per the cell supplier
items.hint: Rule of thumb: leave space for end-of-life swelling as specified by the cell maker. Squeezed cells are a safety and field-return issue.

items.text: Transport and shipping rules for the battery (e.g. UN 38.3, air shipping limits) are identified
items.hint: Shipping certification needs test samples and lead time; confirm requirements with the cell supplier and logistics.

items.text: Battery safety standards for the product category are identified
items.hint: E.g. IEC 62133 for portable cells and packs. Confirm with the compliance lab.

items.text: Venting path and containment for a cell failure are considered in the concept
items.hint: Decide where gases go if a cell vents and keep that path away from the user's face and hands.

items.text: Battery is protected from puncture, crush and sharp edges in the housing
items.hint: Check ribs, screw bosses and metal parts near the cell in CAD; drop loads can drive features into the cell.

items.text: Battery replaceability and access are decided (user, service or none)
items.hint: Drives fasteners, door design and regional battery-removability rules.

items.text: Battery operating and charging temperature limits are reflected in the environmental requirements
items.hint: Charging range is usually narrower than operating range; check against the product's use environment.
